about: Essential Skills 1 (BUSI40009) is a 5-ECTS compulsory Year 1 module in Imperial Business School's BSc Economics, Finance and Data Science, the first of three Essential Skills modules running through the degree. The 2026-entry course page titles it 'Self-awareness and Effective Collaboration', while the 2024-25 programme specification, which places it in the Spring term, called the Year 1 module 'Creative Problem Solving'. No module syllabus or assessment breakdown is published; the programme says skills are assessed through a mix of individual and group coursework (including reports and oral and poster presentations) alongside exams. This guide explains what the module is and how to prepare, without inventing a syllabus.

notes.body:
Essential Skills 1 (BUSI40009) is a 5-ECTS compulsory module in Year 1 of the BSc Economics, Finance and Data Science at Imperial Business School. It is the first of three Essential Skills modules, one in each year, which the programme describes as a dedicated sequence developing the skills employers say they want. In Year 3 the course page talks about completing your "essential skills journey".

The title has changed
- The 2026-entry course page calls it "Essential Skills 1: Self-awareness and Effective Collaboration", and lists "Creative Problem Solving" as Essential Skills 2.
- The 2024-25 programme specification gave the Year 1 module the title "Essential Skills 1: Creative Problem Solving" and Year 2 "Emotional Intelligence in the Workplace".
- So the content has been reorganised between the years. Go by your own module handbook and the module's page on the virtual learning environment for your cohort, not by older descriptions.

What the programme says about these skills (2026-entry course page and 2024-25 specification)
- The course overview mentions specialist modules on effective communication, teamwork and emotional intelligence.
- The programme specification refers to communication and presentation skills, effective teamwork in diverse organisations, a creative mindset to problem solving, and, for Essential Skills 3 in the final year, management skills training focused on Leadership, Ethics, Awareness, Diversity and Societal Impact (LEADS).
- At Level 4 (Year 1) the programme outcomes include transferable skills such as communication, and applying creative thinking to complex, ambiguous problems.

When it runs
The 2024-25 specification places BUSI40009 in the Spring term, alongside Accounting, Microeconomics 1, Macroeconomics 1 and Data Structures and Algorithms. Imperial does not publish a weekly syllabus for this module, so this pack does not invent one.

Why it matters
Group work features in the programme's coursework, and Year 3 centres on a final group project; skills modules like this one are where you learn to work in those teams deliberately rather than by trial and error. They also feed directly into internship and graduate applications, where competency questions ("Tell me about a time you resolved a disagreement in a team") are standard.

Imperial does not publish an assessment breakdown for BUSI40009, so this note only reports what the programme as a whole says. Your module handbook will give the actual components, weights and deadlines.

What the 2024-25 programme specification confirms
- Assessment across the degree mixes individual and group coursework with unseen examinations.
- Coursework types named for the programme include problem sets, project reports, oral presentations and poster presentations, plus in-class or online tests.
- The specification says most modules are weighted mainly towards exams but some are wholly or largely coursework; skills modules are the kind most likely to be coursework-based, but check.
- It also stresses opportunities for feedback and reflection that guide future learning.
- Year 1 counts for 7.5% of the final degree classification, and to progress you must pass all modules for the year (normally 60 ECTS) with an overall weighted average of at least 40%.

What this means in practice
If the module includes reflective writing, group work or presentations (all common in skills modules, though not confirmed here), you are usually judged on:
- the quality of your reflection: specific examples, honest analysis of what happened and why, and a concrete plan for what you will do differently;
- use of relevant concepts or frameworks to explain your experience, not just narration;
- for group outputs, the quality of the shared product and often some evidence of individual contribution (peer assessment is common in group modules);
- for presentations, structure, clarity, timing and handling questions.

Practical habits
- Keep a short log during group work: dates, decisions, who did what, what went well or badly. It makes reflective assignments far easier to write accurately.
- Read the marking criteria before starting, and ask what "reflection" means for this assignment if it is unclear.
- Hit deadlines: late penalties apply to coursework, and in group work a missed deadline affects others.

The 2026 title points to two themes: understanding yourself and working well with others. The frameworks below are widely used in university and workplace teaching on these themes. They are not a confirmed syllabus for BUSI40009, but knowing them will help you write sharper reflections and run better group projects.

Self-awareness
- Johari window (Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham, 1955): four quadrants based on what is known to you and to others: open (known to both), blind (known to others, not you), hidden (known to you, not others) and unknown. Asking for feedback shrinks your blind area; appropriate self-disclosure shrinks your hidden area.
- Emotional intelligence: the ability to perceive, understand and manage your own and others' emotions. The idea was set out by Peter Salovey and John Mayer (1990) and popularised by Daniel Goleman's 1995 book.
- Reflective cycles: Kolb's experiential learning cycle (1984) moves from concrete experience to reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. Gibbs's reflective cycle (1988) has six stages: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan, and is a common structure for reflective essays.

Teams and collaboration
- Tuckman's stages (Bruce Tuckman, 1965): forming, storming, norming and performing; a fifth stage, adjourning, was added with Mary Ann Jensen in 1977. Conflict in the storming stage is normal and can be productive if handled.
- Belbin team roles (Meredith Belbin, Management Teams, 1981): people tend to adopt characteristic roles such as Plant (ideas), Shaper (drive), Monitor Evaluator (critical judgement), Teamworker (harmony), Implementer (getting things done) and Completer Finisher (detail). Balanced teams cover the roles they need.
- Psychological safety (Amy Edmondson, 1999): a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, such as admitting mistakes or asking questions. It is strongly associated with team learning.
- Social loafing: people often put in less effort in groups than alone, especially when individual contributions are invisible. Clear roles and visible individual tasks reduce it.

Giving and receiving feedback
- A simple structure is Situation-Behaviour-Impact: describe when and where, the specific observable behaviour, and its effect, then discuss what to do next.
- Receive feedback by listening, asking clarifying questions and thanking the person before deciding what to act on.

How to prepare
- Before the module, think of two or three real team experiences (school projects, sport, part-time work) you can analyse.
- In your first group project, agree roles, a meeting rhythm, a shared document and a way to resolve disagreements in the first meeting.
- Use frameworks to explain, not decorate: say what happened, why (using the concept) and what you will change.

questions.q: In the Johari window, what is the 'blind' area?
options: Things others know about you that you do not know yourself
Things you know about yourself but keep from others
Things neither you nor others know about you
Things both you and others know about you
questions.why: The blind area is what others see in you that you are unaware of, which is why feedback reduces it. Keeping things from others is the hidden area, what nobody knows is the unknown area, and shared knowledge is the open area.

questions.q: A new project group argues about how to split the work and whose approach to follow. In Tuckman's model, which stage is this, and what does it suggest?
options: Storming: conflict is a normal stage that the group can work through by agreeing roles and norms
Performing: the group has reached full effectiveness
Adjourning: the group is breaking up after completing its task
Forming: members are still polite and uncertain, with no disagreement
questions.why: Disagreement over roles and approach is typical of storming, which Tuckman treated as a normal step before norming. Performing is when a team works effectively with settled roles, adjourning is the ending of the group, and forming is characterised by politeness and uncertainty rather than open conflict.

questions.q: Which approach to feedback follows the Situation-Behaviour-Impact structure?
options: "In Tuesday's meeting you interrupted Sam twice, and he stopped contributing for the rest of the session."
"I think you should be more of a team player."
questions.why: The comment about interrupting Sam in Tuesday's meeting names a specific situation, an observable behaviour and its effect. "Always rude", "be more of a team player" and "everyone thinks you talk too much" are generalisations or judgements about personality with no specific situation or behaviour, which tend to make people defensive and give them nothing concrete to change.
